New to these columns? What every term on this page means — including what a null model is.

Click a column heading to sort; type in the row beneath it to filter. Numeric columns take a comparison (>100, <=-20); a bare number means >=. Everything else matches on substring. Rows with no recorded run sort last and fail every numeric filter.

Rows marked FILL NOT OBTAINABLE are not strategies. Their entry fills on the same bar the signal fires — at that bar's close, or at a limit two ticks under it — which means acting on a price that has not printed yet. They exist to measure how much return that assumption invents, by sitting next to an identical strategy that fills at the next bar's open. On ichimoku_sanyaku the answer is +83 to +130 percentage points, enough to turn −76.8% into +43.9%. Read those rows as the size of a bias, never as a result.

TV and Stockbit count how many of a strategy's conditions each screener can actually express, over its total. Ranking is excluded — no screener does it. A screen built from a partial count returns a superset of the strategy, never a subset, so it is a watchlist builder and not the strategy.

3 Strategies that survive both null models

These pass both the selection and the timing null model. That is the strongest statement this repo makes about a strategy, and it is still one market and one sample.

3.2 ★ screener_ema2_stoch

1d · nulls S✓ T✓ · fwd not_run

Verdict · NOT A FAITHFUL PORT: entry threshold changed from the source's 2% to 5% on the owner's instruction 2026-08-17, against three places in screenersaham that say 2 (docs/AUDIT.md A46). Numbers here are NOT comparable to the source's table. +14.8%, PF 1.060 on 594 trades at a TRADABLE fill (was +19.4%, PF 1.079 at the source's 2%). Re-validated at 5%: survives BOTH null models at N=30 -- selection null median -39.8%, timing null median -51.6%, 0 of 30 beat it in either (p ~ 0.032), and its -34.0% drawdown beats all 30 random baskets. STILL NOT DEPLOYABLE: REGIME-DEPENDENT, typical trade loses in every period. Forward-test first.

short_ema_dist_pct <= 5

A minimum taken across four EMAs at once, and no screener exposes a distance-to-nearest-of-N-averages field. CORRECTED 2026-08-17. This entry used to say the clause "cannot be assembled from separate rules because the min is over the four, not each of them". That reasoning is wrong: `min(d3,d5,d10,d20) <= 2` is exactly `d3 <= 2 OR d5 <= 2 OR d10 <= 2 OR d20 <= 2`, so it decomposes perfectly. Two real blockers sit behind it instead. (1) A screener ANDs its filters. There is no OR across rules, so the four-way disjunction needs FOUR separate screen runs whose results are unioned by hand -- possible, but it is not one recipe. (2) Each disjunct is a BOUNDED band on price versus one EMA ("above EMA(N) and no more than 2% above it"). The upper half of that band needs "Manual setup", which meta.tradingview.limits records as requiring sign-in and NOT verified. The "Below Price" preset gives only the lower half. Measured, so the size of the gap is known. Taking the ema_3 leg alone is a strict SUBSET of the real clause: it admits 0 bars the clause rejects, and at the threshold these presets currently run (5%) it misses 1,638 of 323,386 -- 0.5%. ema_3 is the highest of the four on 85.1% of bars where price is above all of them, which is why one leg gets so close, and a wider band makes the distinction matter less still (at the source's own 2% the same leg missed 6,535 of 264,191, 2.5%). Both figures are recorded because the threshold is an owner-set deviation from the source and may revert -- see docs/AUDIT.md A46. A subset is the WRONG direction for this file regardless: a recipe must be a superset or it hides real candidates. So this is documented and deliberately not shipped as the mapping, even at 0.5%. This is the condition that makes the screenersaham presets selective, so a recipe without it is a much wider list than the strategy -- see docs/SCREENERSAHAM.md.

stoch_rsi_14 <= 20

The filter exists and is the WRONG INDICATOR, which is worse than a missing one. Read directly on 2026-08-17: TradingView's "Stochastic RSI" carries parameters 3,3,14,14 -- the leading 3,3 are the %K and %D smoothing lengths. idxbt's stoch_rsi_14 is the RAW unsmoothed value (docs/METRICS.md). Its "K below 20 / Oversold (%K)" preset therefore neither implies nor is implied by stoch_rsi_14 <= 20, so it is not a valid widening and would break the superset guarantee this whole approach rests on.

Then rank by value_traded_20 — highest first, keep 10. No screener does this step, and it is not counted above.

Same disjunction problem as TradingView (see above), plus a harder one: Stockbit's rule shape `[field] [op] [multiplier] x [field]` would express one leg exactly as "Price <= 1.02 x Price EMA 3" -- but Stockbit has no EMA at all. Its `Price MA N` is the SIMPLE average, already mapped to the `sma_*` terms, so pointing this term at it would be the same class of error as the Stoch RSI trap below.

rsi_14 >= 50

Filter: Relative strength index

Period defaults to 14, which is the one this term means, and idxbt uses Wilder's RSI as TradingView does -- so the readings should agree closely. BUT the presets are one-sided: Above 90/80/70/60 and Below 40/30/20. A band like "rsi_14 between 50 and 70" cannot be set from them; the nearest valid WIDENING is "Above 40", which is a superset of >= 50 and keeps the screen a superset of the strategy. An exact bound needs "Manual setup", which requires signing in and is not verified.

Period defaults to 14, which is the one this term means, and idxbt uses Wilder's RSI as TradingView does -- so the readings should agree closely. A band like "rsi_14 between 50 and 70" cannot be set from them; the nearest valid WIDENING is "Above 40", which is a superset of >= 50 and keeps the screen a superset of the strategy. Not applied by the screen

short_ema_dist_pct <= 5

A minimum taken across four EMAs at once, and no screener exposes a distance-to-nearest-of-N-averages field. CORRECTED 2026-08-17. This entry used to say the clause "cannot be assembled from separate rules because the min is over the four, not each of them". That reasoning is wrong: `min(d3,d5,d10,d20) <= 2` is exactly `d3 <= 2 OR d5 <= 2 OR d10 <= 2 OR d20 <= 2`, so it decomposes perfectly. Two real blockers sit behind it instead. (1) A screener ANDs its filters. There is no OR across rules, so the four-way disjunction needs FOUR separate screen runs whose results are unioned by hand -- possible, but it is not one recipe. (2) Each disjunct is a BOUNDED band on price versus one EMA ("above EMA(N) and no more than 2% above it"). The upper half of that band needs "Manual setup", which meta.tradingview.limits records as requiring sign-in and NOT verified. The "Below Price" preset gives only the lower half. Measured, so the size of the gap is known. Taking the ema_3 leg alone is a strict SUBSET of the real clause: it admits 0 bars the clause rejects, and at the threshold these presets currently run (5%) it misses 1,638 of 323,386 -- 0.5%. ema_3 is the highest of the four on 85.1% of bars where price is above all of them, which is why one leg gets so close, and a wider band makes the distinction matter less still (at the source's own 2% the same leg missed 6,535 of 264,191, 2.5%). Both figures are recorded because the threshold is an owner-set deviation from the source and may revert -- see docs/AUDIT.md A46. A subset is the WRONG direction for this file regardless: a recipe must be a superset or it hides real candidates. So this is documented and deliberately not shipped as the mapping, even at 0.5%. This is the condition that makes the screenersaham presets selective, so a recipe without it is a much wider list than the strategy -- see docs/SCREENERSAHAM.md.

Then rank by value_traded_20 — highest first, keep 10. No screener does this step, and it is not counted above.

A minimum taken across four EMAs at once, and no screener exposes a distance-to-nearest-of-N-averages field. CORRECTED 2026-08-17. This entry used to say the clause "cannot be assembled from separate rules because the min is over the four, not each of them". That reasoning is wrong: `min(d3,d5,d10,d20) <= 2` is exactly `d3 <= 2 OR d5 <= 2 OR d10 <= 2 OR d20 <= 2`, so it decomposes perfectly. Two real blockers sit behind it instead. (1) A screener ANDs its filters. There is no OR across rules, so the four-way disjunction needs FOUR separate screen runs whose results are unioned by hand -- possible, but it is not one recipe. (2) Each disjunct is a BOUNDED band on price versus one EMA ("above EMA(N) and no more than 2% above it"). The upper half of that band needs "Manual setup", which meta.tradingview.limits records as requiring sign-in and NOT verified. The "Below Price" preset gives only the lower half. Measured, so the size of the gap is known. Taking the ema_3 leg alone is a strict SUBSET of the real clause: it admits 0 bars the clause rejects, and at the threshold these presets currently run (5%) it misses 1,638 of 323,386 -- 0.5%. ema_3 is the highest of the four on 85.1% of bars where price is above all of them, which is why one leg gets so close, and a wider band makes the distinction matter less still (at the source's own 2% the same leg missed 6,535 of 264,191, 2.5%). Both figures are recorded because the threshold is an owner-set deviation from the source and may revert -- see docs/AUDIT.md A46. A subset is the WRONG direction for this file regardless: a recipe must be a superset or it hides real candidates. So this is documented and deliberately not shipped as the mapping, even at 0.5%. This is the condition that makes the screenersaham presets selective, so a recipe without it is a much wider list than the strategy -- see docs/SCREENERSAHAM.md.

stoch_rsi_14 <= 20

The filter exists and is the WRONG INDICATOR, which is worse than a missing one. Read directly on 2026-08-17: TradingView's "Stochastic RSI" carries parameters 3,3,14,14 -- the leading 3,3 are the %K and %D smoothing lengths. idxbt's stoch_rsi_14 is the RAW unsmoothed value (docs/METRICS.md). Its "K below 20 / Oversold (%K)" preset therefore neither implies nor is implied by stoch_rsi_14 <= 20, so it is not a valid widening and would break the superset guarantee this whole approach rests on.

Then rank by value_traded_20 — highest first, keep 10. No screener does this step, and it is not counted above.

5 Terms and definitions

Every term the table and the sections above put on screen, in plain language — including what each one does not tell you, which is usually the part that matters.

The one that confuses everyone

Null model
A test of whether a result could have come from luck. The engine re-runs the strategy many times with one ingredient deliberately destroyed, keeping everything else identical — same exits, same costs, same IDX trading rules — and then asks where the real result lands among the fakes. If the real run is not clearly better than the random ones, the ingredient that was destroyed was not doing any work.

There are two of them here, and a strategy is only starred when it survives both. Passing one is common; passing both is not.
Selection null S
Keeps every entry date exactly as the strategy chose it, and randomises which eligible stocks were bought on those days.

It answers: is the stock-picking rule better than drawing names out of a hat on the same days? If random names on the same dates earn about the same, the entry rule is decorative and the market filter deciding when is doing all the work.
Seen as: S✓ passed · S✗ failed · S– never run
Timing null T
Randomises the entry dates — and the names, and ignores the market filter entirely.

It answers: is entering on these particular days better than entering on random days? This is the harder one to pass, and the one most strategies here fail. Failing it usually means the strategy was riding the market rather than timing it.
Seen as: T✓ passed · T✗ failed · T– never run
p-value
How often a random run matched or beat the real one. p≈.03 means about 3% of the fakes did as well — lower is stronger evidence.

It has a floor set by how many times the test was run. With N random runs the smallest p that can possibly be reported is 1/(N+1), so 12 runs cannot produce anything below .077 no matter how good the strategy is. A weak-looking p from a short run is not evidence of a weak strategy; it is evidence of a short run.
Forward test
Re-running the strategy on a slice of time that was deliberately held back, to see whether it still works on data it was not built against.

clean — the held-back period really was unseen when the strategy was written.
contaminated — it was not. The strategy was designed after its author had already looked at that period, so the test is a consistency check and not evidence about the future. Recorded rather than hidden, because a contaminated test that looks like a clean one is worse than none.
not_run — no forward test has been done.
Seen as: fwd clean · fwd contaminated · fwd not_run

Reading the table

★ (star)
This strategy survived both null models. It is the strongest statement this project makes about any strategy, and it still means one market, one sample, and a result that has not been traded.
TF — timeframe
Which bars the strategy runs on. 1d is daily, 1wk weekly. It matters more than it looks: a "50-period moving average" is 50 days on one and 50 weeks — nearly a year — on the other.
Seen as: 1d · 1wk
Return %
Total growth of the account over the whole backtest, from first bar to last. Not annualised, so a 180% over six years and a 180% over one year read identically here. Net of modelled costs.
Max DD % — maximum drawdown
The deepest peak-to-trough fall the account went through, as a percentage. Always negative. −35 means that at its worst the account was down 35% from its previous high.

This is the number that decides whether a strategy is actually holdable. A return you cannot sit through is not a return you will earn.
Profit factor
Gross profit divided by gross loss. Above 1.00 makes money; 2.00 means it won twice as much as it lost in total.

It says nothing about distribution — a 2.00 built from one enormous winner and a hundred small losses is a different animal from a 2.00 built from steady small wins, and this column cannot tell them apart.
Trades
How many positions were opened and closed. Small numbers make every other column on the row unreliable: twenty trades is not enough to distinguish a strategy from luck, whatever its return says.
Costs % cap
Everything paid to trade — commission, fees, and the 0.1% Indonesian sell tax — totalled over the whole run and expressed as a percentage of the starting capital.

It can exceed 100% and that is not a bug: a strategy that turns over its capital many times pays the round trip many times. A high number next to a high return means the gross edge had to be large to survive its own trading.
Run date
When this strategy's backtest was last actually executed. Results are files on disk; this is how old they are.
no run recorded
This strategy has never been backtested, or its results were deleted. The row is deliberately blank rather than zero — an unknown is never shown as a result.

Warnings on a row

STALE
This strategy's saved results are older than the price data they would run on. The numbers describe a previous version of the data and must be re-run before being quoted.
FILL NOT OBTAINABLE
This strategy's entry fills on the same bar the signal fires, at or below a closing price that had not printed yet when the decision was made. Its return could not have been earned by anyone. Marked in the table rather than only in its own section, because the table sorts by return and an unearnable row otherwise lands among the winners.

Screening

TV and Stockbit columns
How many of the strategy's entry conditions that screener can actually express, out of the total. 4 / 8 means four of its eight rules can be set up as filters there and four cannot.

A partial screen returns a superset: it can hand you extra names but never hides a real one. That is what makes it safe to use as a watchlist builder — and why it is not the strategy.
Seen as: 4 / 8 · 0 / 6
rank_by
A screen returns a set of eligible names; a strategy holds only its best few, chosen by ranking them on one column. No screener performs this step, and it is deliberately excluded from the fraction above.

For a strategy whose entry rule is a loose floor, this ranking is the selection — so a high screener fraction on such a strategy is flattering rather than informative.
Market gate
A condition on the index rather than on any single stock, such as "only trade while the IHSG is above its own 50-day average". It decides whether the strategy takes any new position today at all, so it is checked once on a ^JKSE chart rather than being a filter in the screener.

The chart

Equity curve
The account balance over time — what the strategy would have been worth on each date.
Rebased to 100
Every curve is scaled so that it starts at 100, so strategies that began at different times and sizes can be compared by shape. A curve reaching 250 has grown 150%. The index line is clipped to the same window and rebased the same way, so it answers "would you have done better just buying the index".
log y / linear y
The vertical scale. On a log axis equal vertical distances are equal percentage moves, which is what makes a dozen curves spanning 100 to 1600 readable at once. On a linear axis they are equal rupiah moves, which makes the largest curve dominate.

Appearance

Colour
Width
